extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners (attorneys and agents) drafting claims
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for drafting patent claims that recite elements in combination, contrasting Superguide ("at least one of A, B, or C") and Markush ("selected from the group consisting of A, B, and C") constructions and their syntactic and indefiniteness risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Superguide construction — use of 'or' to claim combinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the SuperGuide approach: test whether the claim recites "OR" or "AND" when listing a series of elements. "At least one of A, B, or C" is interpreted to permit combinations of the elements; by contrast, "at least one of A, B, and C" is interpreted as requiring at least one A, at least one B, and at least one C.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical test: does your claim recite "OR" (combination-allowing) or "AND" (requires each element)? See SuperGuide Corp. v. DirecTV Enters., Inc., 358 F.3d 870 (Fed. Cir. 2004). To claim combinations straightforwardly, use wording like "at least one of A, B, or C."

rubrics_metrics.name: Markush construction — default presumption of single-member selection
rubrics_metrics.description: A Markush claim that recites "a member selected from the group consisting of A, B, and C" is presumed to permit the member to be one and only one of A, B, or C, and to exclude mixtures or combinations of A, B, and C.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because Markush groupings are by nature closed and presume single-member selection, drafters should not expect a plain Markush recitation to cover combinations or mixtures without additional qualifying language. See Multilayer Stretch Cling Film Holdings, Inc. v. Berry Plastics Corp., 831 F.3d 1350, 1363 (Fed. Cir. 2016) and MPEP 2173.05(h).

rubrics_metrics.name: To encompass combinations or mixtures in a Markush group, add qualifying language
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim is intended to encompass combinations or mixtures of the alternatives set forth in the Markush grouping, the claim may include qualifying language preceding the recited alternatives (such as "at least one member" selected from the group), or within the list of alternatives (such as "or mixtures thereof").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example modifications: (1) "at least one X selected from the group consisting of A, B, and C" (to recite combinations); (2) "an X selected from the group consisting of A, B, and C, or mixtures thereof" (to recite mixtures). See MPEP 2173.05(h) (citing Abbott Labs v. Baxter Pharmaceutical Products, Inc., 334 F.3d 1274, 1281 (Fed. Cir. 2003)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper Markush syntax — use the transitional phrase 'group consisting of' to close the group
rubrics_metrics.description: A Markush grouping is a closed group of alternatives and requires the transitional phrase "group consisting of" rather than "group of," "comprising," or "including." Without "consisting," the phrase is presumptively open and the PTO will insist on adding "consisting of" to ensure a closed meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the transition phrase "group consisting of" in Markush claims to avoid issues with open language. The PTO will typically insist on "consisting of" to close the group; failure to include it risks later §112(b) indefiniteness challenges. See Abbott Labs. v. Baxter Pharm. Prods., Inc., 334 F.3d 1274, 1280 (Fed. Cir. 2003) and Gillette Co. v. Energizer Holdings, Inc., 405 F.3d 1367, 1372 (Fed. Cir. 2005).

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of §112(b) indefiniteness and court review for improperly formed Markush syntax
rubrics_metrics.description: Reciting a Markush claim without proper syntax (e.g., omitting "consisting of") raises the risk that the Patent Office might fail to spot the missing language and that the claim's definiteness under 35 U.S.C. §112(b) may later be reviewed by the courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts evaluate definiteness in light of the specification; while it is the PTO's job to ensure a claim is definite and that Markush expressions are used properly on examination, district courts reviewing indefiniteness assess the claim language and written description, not simply whether the PTO made a technical error. Take care in claim drafting and ensure specification support to mitigate later indefiniteness challenges. See Lexington Luminance LLC v. Amazon.com Inc., 601 F. App'x 963, 968 (Fed. Cir. 2015).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical drafting recommendation — prefer Superguide or properly formed Markush for combinations
rubrics_metrics.description: To recite elements in combination while avoiding Markush complexity, practitioners may use the Superguide syntax (e.g., "at least one of A, B, or C"). Alternatively, when using a Markush group, use the proper closed form syntax such as "at least one X selected from a group consisting of A, B, and C."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendation: use Superguide wording for straightforward combination coverage. If electing Markush, explicitly include "at least one" and the transition "consisting of" to avoid inadvertent narrowing or indefiniteness and to reduce the likelihood a court will have to address an improperly formed Markush that slipped by the PTO.
